newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Aerospatial alliance possible - Matra Marconi chief.
newsitem.headline: Aerospatial alliance possible - Matra Marconi chief.

text.p: A strategic alliance between Matra Marconia Space (MMS) and Italian-state owned Aerospatial could help build a European satellite maker big enough to rival U.S. giants, MMS chief Armand Carlier said on Thursday.
"It is better for European forces to be gathered in one place rather than fighting against each other," Carlier told a news conference at the Asia Telecom 97 trade show.
Carlier said he would not rule out buying some or all of Aerospatial, describing the idea as "a long term possibility".
A takeover bid for French state-owned Thomson-CSF by MMS is now in serious doubt after a Socialist general election victory earlier this month.
The Socialist election platform promised to scrap all privatisations of French industry.

"If the (Italian) state wanted to privatise its activities in space, as a long-term possibility we have said we would be happy to play a role in this," Carlier said, adding that facilities sharing was an immediate short term option.

"They (Aerospatial) have a very nice installation for building satellites in Cannes. At the moment we are very busy and at some point they may be less busy. It is possible that we can have some utilisation of their facility and plant, but that sort of thing can be done at arm's length," Carlier said.

The Anglo-French company, owned 51 percent by Lagardere Groupe and 49 percent by General Electric Co Plc , is in the process of adding German capability to its operations through the acquisition of Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG .
The deal announced in May would give MMS, likely to be renamed Matra Marconi Dasa (MMD) after the sale is approved by shareholders, annual sales of US$3 billion.
This would rank it the third biggest satellite maker behind Lockheed Martin with US$7 billion and the newly merged Boeing McDonnell Douglas with US$5 billion.
MMD would be able to save about 30 percent of its costs while adding manufacturing capability that would enable it to make about 60 percent of its satellites in-house, Carlier said.
